title: Type Guards
subtitle: typeof, instanceof, in, user-defined predicates (x is T), and assertion functions
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: TypeScript's type narrowing works automatically for simple typeof/instanceof checks, but complex validation logic (checking an API response matches an interface) isn't automatically recognized. TypeScript needs a way to trust your validation logic.
whyItExists.solution: Type predicates: a function with return type x is T. When the function returns true, TypeScript narrows x to T in the true branch. Assertion functions: asserts x is T — after calling the function, TypeScript treats x as T in the calling scope.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Whenever you validate an unknown/any value from an external source (API, user input, localStorage) and want TypeScript to recognize the narrowed type. Also for reusable narrowing logic.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use assertion functions as a shortcut to cast types without validating — that's the same as using as T, which bypasses safety. The predicate function must actually check the type.

explainModes.beginner: A type guard is a function that checks if a value is a specific type and tells TypeScript about the result. You write it once, and TypeScript trusts it everywhere you use it. Instead of repeating typeof x === 'string' checks, you write isString(x) and TypeScript knows that after the check, x is a string.
explainModes.simple: typeof x === 'string' — built-in narrowing. x instanceof MyClass — narrows to MyClass. 'prop' in x — narrows to types with that property. User-defined predicate: function isUser(x: unknown): x is User { return ... }. Assertion function: function assertUser(x: unknown): asserts x is User { if (!isUser(x)) throw new Error(); }.
explainModes.standard: Type predicates work with if/else, ternary, and filter. isString is treated as () => x is string — when it returns true, TypeScript narrows. Array narrowing: array.filter(isUser) — the result type is User[] (not (User | OtherType)[]). Assertion functions: after calling assertUser(x), TypeScript knows x is User — even without an if check. They're useful in constructor validation and express-style middleware.
explainModes.technical: Type predicate syntax requires specifying which parameter is narrowed: function isA(x: A | B): x is A. Multiple predicates with intersection: rarely needed — TypeScript doesn't support x is A & B in predicate syntax directly. Discriminant-based guard: function isCircle(s: Shape): s is Circle { return s.kind === 'circle' } — often redundant if you're already using switch (s.kind). Custom guard with assertion: function assert(cond: unknown, msg?: string): asserts cond { if (!cond) throw new Error(msg) }.
explainModes.deepDive: Type predicates are not verified by TypeScript — you can write function isString(x: unknown): x is string { return true; } and TypeScript will trust it even though it's wrong. This is intentional: TypeScript gives you a way to push knowledge about runtime behavior into the type system, with the responsibility of correctness on you. Composing predicates: function isActiveUser(x: unknown): x is ActiveUser { return isUser(x) && x.status === 'active' }. Assertion function types: asserts condition, asserts value is T — both exist in the TS stdlib.

questions.question: Why is `items.filter(isUser)` typed as `User[]` when `isUser` is a type predicate?
options: TypeScript automatically infers the type from the filter callback
The type predicate return type `x is User` tells TypeScript that when isUser returns true, the element is User — Array.filter uses this to narrow the result array type
The result is always User[] regardless of the predicate return type
filter() always returns the element type of the input array
questions.explanation: TypeScript's Array.filter signature has an overload specifically for type predicates: filter<S extends T>(predicate: (value: T) => value is S): S[]. When you pass a type predicate function (x: unknown): x is User, TypeScript uses the S type (User) as the return array's element type. Without a type predicate, filter returns the same type as the input array.

faq.q: Can I write a wrong type predicate? Does TypeScript catch it?
faq.a: Yes, you can write a lying predicate — TypeScript doesn't verify that your predicate actually checks the right thing. function isString(x: unknown): x is string { return true } would compile. TypeScript trusts you. This is intentional: some runtime checks are too complex for the type system to verify. The responsibility for correctness is yours. Use libraries like zod or io-ts for validated type narrowing.

examples: function isApiError(x: unknown): x is ApiError { return x instanceof Error && 'code' in x }
function requireAuth(req: Request): asserts req is AuthenticatedRequest { if (!req.user) throw new UnauthorizedError() }
